ct_nells_rock_walking_trails.blurb: A network of public woodland trails in Shelton where boulders sit scattered along the paths, with problems spread over several small clusters and a larger field higher up the hill. The climbing is all bouldering, and most problems fall between V2 and V4, with a handful of harder lines up to V7 for strong climbers. Classics include Surge, Clockwork Orange and Creamsicle at the harder end, and Port Side or Make Way for Ducklings for an easier warm-up. Because it is a walking-trail system, expect dog walkers and hikers passing by. Bring pads, since landings can be uneven.
ct_nells_rock_walking_trails.parking_note: A small lot sits right on Nells Rock Road in front of the trailheads, just south of the Shelton dog park.
ct_nells_rock_walking_trails.approach: An easy stroll from the lot: one path heads left and another goes straight into the trees, with boulders along both.

ct_laddin_s_rock.blurb: A small, shady wooded crag in Old Greenwich with a wall of roughly 60 feet, a few short boulders and a mostly trad selection of routes. The grades center on 5.10, with easier lines and a sprinkling of harder ones, and First Aid is the best-known 5.10a. Fixed anchors top several lines and everything can be top-roped, which makes it a handy spot for climbers moving from the gym to real rock. The forest canopy keeps it cool, but some sections stay damp from runoff, so give it time after rain. Pack out any trash you find.
ct_laddin_s_rock.parking_note: Use the Rosa Hartman lot on Brown House Road, on the Stamford side of the sanctuary.
ct_laddin_s_rock.approach: From the lot, follow the trail west and then north until the wall comes into view across a small drainage.

ct_main_slab.blurb: The most visited crag at Whitestone Cliffs in Mattatuck State Forest, a south-west facing gneiss slab about 80 feet wide with routes 40 to 60 feet long. The angle is lower on the right and steeper on the left, and the grades run from about 5.4 to 5.10, with the most common in the 5.7 to 5.8 range. Most lines take gear, and every one can be rigged as a top-rope, though many trees near the edge have died, so bring long webbing or a static rope for anchors. Nectar of the Gods and Super Stout, both 5.9, are the standouts.
ct_main_slab.parking_note: From Spruce Brook Road, a gravel pull-off on the left about 1.3 miles in holds five or six cars; watch for the rock sticking up in its middle.
ct_main_slab.approach: Pass the barrier and climb a rocky jeep track, then join the blue-blazed trail and follow it uphill over a scramble to the cliffs. A short climbers' path drops to the base of the slab.

ct_rattlesnake_cliff.blurb: A wooded trap rock cliff on Rattlesnake Mountain in Farmington, with mostly trad climbing plus a few top-rope lines. The most common grades sit around 5.7 to 5.8, with some 5.10s and 5.11s for stronger climbers; Down-to-Earth, Slip Knot and Twister are the ones to know. The cliff faces south and catches the sun through the afternoon, which makes it a pleasant place on cold days. In summer the mosquitoes can be relentless and the right side tends to seep. A boulder cave beside the ridge trail is worth a look.
ct_rattlesnake_cliff.approach: Follow the ridge-top Metacomet Trail north until the crag appears; if you reach Greenwall you have walked too far.

ct_main_walls.blurb: The principal cliffs of Cathole Mountain in Meriden, a trap rock ridge with routes from the lower 5.5s up into the 5.12 range, though the bulk sit between 5.9 and 5.11. Trad leading dominates, with a handful of top-rope lines. Pegasus, Arrowhead and Fool's Mate are popular trad lines, while Jaguar is a well-liked 5.10+ top rope. The rock is known for loose pieces, so wear a helmet. The walk is short but steep and loose, and trees for anchors sit well back from the edge, so bring long webbing.

ga_panola_area_1.blurb: A shady bouldering zone in the woods of Panola Mountain, southeast of Atlanta, with problems ranging from easy slabs to V8. Most fall between V0 and V5, mixing slabs, arêtes, cracks and traverses. Quartz, Creeping Death and The Granite Rose 2.0 are the classics, plus easier fun like Bittens McDangerfeet and Brush Your Teeth. Tree cover keeps the area cool for most of the day, which suits warmer months. Bring a couple of pads and plan on a modest walk in.
ga_panola_area_1.parking_note: Park in the Alexander Lake lot inside the state park.
ga_panola_area_1.approach: Walk the paved path northwest between the two lakes, then turn onto a blazed footpath through the trees to reach the boulders.

ga_main_face.blurb: The largest and longest cliff on Mount Yonah, a granite dome in the north Georgia mountains. It is mostly trad, with a few bolted lines and the longest climbs on the mountain, including some multi-pitch. Many routes are in the 5.5 to 5.6 range, with a good spread up through 5.9 and a handful of 5.11s and 5.12s. Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds, Special Edition and Stannard's Crack are the standouts. The face points southwest and bakes in summer, so spring and fall are kinder. Numbered, color-marked lines and extra bolts remain from past military training. Watch for loose debris from above.

ga_main_wall_2.blurb: The headline cliff of Tallulah Gorge, a deep quartzite chasm in northeast Georgia. Nearly all the climbing is steep trad, often multi-pitch, with a few aid lines; most routes are 5.10 or harder, and a lot are 5.11 and 5.12. Mescaline Daydream and Primitive Paradox are among the more approachable lines, while Punk Wave, Rapture of the Steep and Highly Wired draw stronger parties. The wall is serious and exposed. The base is reached by a short, committing downclimb on a fixed rope and a creek crossing, and snakes are common in warm months.
ga_main_wall_2.parking_note: Use the lot at the park's interpretive center, where the trail into the gorge begins.

ga_brick_wall.blurb: The steepest and shortest of the walls at Currahee Mountain near Toccoa, a small granite crag with a mix of sport routes, a little trad and some boulder problems. The routes are mostly 5.10 to 5.12, with the 5.11s most common, and the climbing is crimpy and pumpy. Plague, Jeep Streak, Ebola and Comfortably Numb are the draws. The wall only gets afternoon sun, so it works on warmer days. Most lines can be top-roped, though some bolted ones must be led first.
ga_brick_wall.parking_note: Drive the gravel road to the summit and park by the towers, though it gets rough after rain; or park at the pull-through at the mountain's base and hike about a mile.
ga_brick_wall.approach: From the tower lot, take the trail on the right side and bear left under the cliffs; Brick Wall is the leftmost of three walls.

ga_phantom_area.blurb: One of the most popular bouldering zones at Zahnd, a small natural area on Lookout Mountain in northwest Georgia. The sandstone is gray and pebbly, a bit rough on skin, with good features. There are problems from V0 to V10, with most in the V3 to V6 range. The Turret, Razors Edge, Razorback, Harvest Moon and Pray Like a Mantis are the best known. It is quieter than the busier Georgia boulder fields, so bring pads and a partner to spot.
ga_phantom_area.parking_note: Use the marked pull-offs near the trailhead and carpool where you can.
ga_phantom_area.approach: Follow the main trail a couple hundred yards to a fork, then take the right branch a short way downhill to the boulders.
